how-to-price-lawn-mowing.html.text:
← Lawn care bid calculator

How to price lawn mowing without a per-acre guess

Operators search for “how to price lawn mowing” because the numbers they find — $40 a half-acre, $50 a front yard — cannot see the stop they are actually running. Two lots of the same size are not the same job.

Split the stop into services

Open turf mows fast. Beds, hedges, and a careful edge do not. Time each service from your own crew: square feet of turf per hour, minutes of edging and blowing, square feet of beds. Hours on the property are those quantities divided by those rates. A 10,000 sq ft lawn at 20,000 sq ft per hour is a 30-minute mow. The same lot with 350 sq ft of beds at 400 sq ft per hour is another 50 minutes before anyone starts the truck.

Count windshield time as labor

Round-trip drive time is paid time. On a suburban route an 18-minute one-way hop is 36 minutes on every visit — often more than the mow. A price-per-acre rule never adds it. Fuel and dump fees sit on top of the same visit.

Do not invent winter

In-season monthly is weekly visits times 52/12 weeks, not a flat four. Annual is the per-visit price times the growing-season weeks you actually bill — commonly the high 20s to mid 30s in temperate US climates, not twelve months. Quoting monthly × 12 either overcharges a homeowner who wants a year-round number or undercharges you if you skip winter.

Open the lawn care bid calculator, replace the starting rates with numbers timed from your crew, and read the walk-away price before you sharpen the pencil. The page is arithmetic on your inputs, not a recommended price.

Common questions

How do I price a lawn mowing job?

Split the stop into services and time each one from your own crew rather than using a per-acre rule. A 10,000 sq ft lawn at 20,000 sq ft per hour is a 30-minute mow, and the same lot with 350 sq ft of beds at 400 sq ft per hour is another 50 minutes before anyone starts the truck. Add round-trip drive time as paid labor, then fuel and dump fees on the same visit.

How do I turn a per-visit mowing price into a monthly or annual price?

In-season monthly is weekly visits times 52/12 weeks, not a flat four. Annual is the per-visit price times the growing-season weeks you actually bill, commonly the high 20s to mid 30s in temperate US climates, not twelve months. Quoting monthly times twelve either overcharges a homeowner who wants a year-round number or undercharges you if you skip winter.

No warranty. This is not legal, tax, financial, or business advice. Verify every figure against your own costs before relying on it or submitting a bid.

FOR INDEPENDENT LAWN CARE OPERATORS

Bid the stop, not the lot size.

Price a recurring lawn-care stop the way a crew actually runs it: turf, beds, and edging each at their own production rate, then windshield time, fuel, dump, and the margin you intend to keep. You get the price per visit, the in-season monthly, an annual that counts growing-season weeks rather than inventing winter, and the number below which the stop loses money.

Background: how to price lawn mowing without a per-acre guess · This calculator vs. a flat rate per acre · This calculator vs. LMN by Granum.

The property

One row per service on the visit. Production rate is how much one person covers per hour in that row’s unit. Pick a service to start from a common figure, then replace it with a rate timed from your own crew.

ServiceQuantityPer hour

Route and season

Round-trip travel is loaded labor. Service weeks are the growing season you actually bill — 32 is a common temperate-US figure, not a recommendation. Annual is visit price × these weeks, not monthly × 12.

Your costs

Payroll burden covers employer taxes, workers’ compensation, and paid time off. Equipment share is this stop’s piece of the mower payment, trailer, and shop — not the whole fleet.

Where the hours go

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. The starting production rates are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard, a benchmark, or a guarantee — time your own crews and replace them.

    Hand the customer a proposal

    The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

    Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

    Common questions

    How do I price lawn mowing for a residential yard?

    Split the stop into services with their own rates — turf mowing, edging and blowing, beds — then add round-trip travel, fuel, and dump. Price from those hours plus overhead and the margin you intend to keep, not from lot size alone.

    Why is a price per acre a bad lawn care bid?

    Two half-acre lots are not the same job. Beds, hedges, and an 18-minute drive each way often take more of the stop than the mow. A flat per-acre rule cannot see any of that.

    Should a lawn care contract be monthly times twelve?

    Only if you actually service the property every month. Most growing-season routes run 28 to 36 weeks. Annual is the per-visit price times those weeks, not the in-season monthly times twelve.

    Why doesn’t adding a second crew member change the price?

    Crew size only splits the clock time on site — how fast the stop gets done — not the cost. Labor is priced on total person-hours of work, and that total doesn’t shrink because two people share it. On the starting figures (10,000 sq ft turf, 25 minutes of edging, 350 sq ft of beds), one crew member clocks 1.79 hours on the property; a two-person crew clocks 0.90 hours to do the same work, but the bill stays $459.73 in-season monthly either way. A second person buys you a shorter stop and more stops per day, not a smaller number on this page — unless you also raise the wage field for a second body on the truck.

    What’s the difference between “In-season monthly” and “Year-round monthly equivalent”?

    “In-season monthly” is what the stop actually bills during the weeks you show up — on the starting figures, $459.73 across the 32 growing-season weeks. “Year-round monthly equivalent” ($282.91 at those same figures) spreads the honest annual total evenly across all 12 months instead, which is the number to quote a customer who wants one flat payment in January and August alike. Both come from the same annual total; only the billing pattern differs.

    How much of the bid is travel time, not yard work?

    Round-trip drive time counts as labor on every visit, and it can be a bigger share than any single service line. At an 18-minute one-way drive, travel is 0.6 hours of the 2.39-hour visit — about 25% of the billed time, more than either the edging or the bed-weeding line on the starting figures. A route with a short drive and a route with a long one doing identical yard work should not carry the same price; this field is why they don’t.

    What does the calculator say if I quote below the walk-away price?

    Type a number into “Monthly price you’re considering” and the verdict box compares it to the walk-away monthly (your cost with zero margin) and flags it red if it’s under. At the starting figures the walk-away is $344.80/month; a $90 quote shows a $254.80 monthly loss before the owner takes anything out of it — the field exists so that number shows up before the contract is signed, not after the season is half over.

vs-a-flat-rate-per-acre.html.text:
← Lawn Care Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat rate per acre

“$800 an acre, mowed weekly” is not a price for a lawn-care stop — it is a price for one lot's worth of beds, edging, and drive time, quietly applied to every lot after it.

What a flat rate per acre is

A flat per-acre rate is the fastest way to quote a recurring mowing stop: measure the lot, multiply by a number. Customers shop it because it is easy to compare between crews, and it is the figure a homeowner holding a competitor's flyer will ask you to match.

The rate behind it was set for one kind of lot — usually open turf, no beds to weed, no edge-and-blow, and a short hop from the stop before it — and then reused for every lot afterward, whether or not the next one carries beds, a full edge, or sits a long drive away.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter each service's quantity and production rate — turf, edging, beds, hedges, leaf cleanup — your visits per week, service weeks per year, round-trip travel, and your own wage, payroll burden, fuel, dump, equipment, overhead, and target margin. It prices the mowing hours from a turf-specific rate, adds beds, edging, and travel as their own buckets, and returns the price per visit, the in-season monthly, and the walk-away price — for this lot, not a flat rate for every acre.

What a flat rate per acre doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same monthly rate whether the lot is open turf or carries beds that extract at a slower square-foot-per-hour rate. Prices mowing hours from a turf-specific production rate, and bed weeding from its own slower rate, so a lot with more bed area costs more without anyone eyeballing a surcharge.
Has no line for edging and blowing at all — a lot with a full edge gets the same quote as one with none. Prices edging and blowing in minutes you set, as a first-class service line rather than a habit folded into the mow.
Quotes the same rate for a stop next door and one an 18-minute drive away, with no separate line for the travel. Prices round-trip travel as paid labor at the minutes you set, so a far stop is never quoted at the near stop's rate.
Multiplies a single rate by acreage and calls that the price, whatever the season length or visit count. Turns visits per week and service weeks per year into an honest in-season monthly and annual, not a flat rate times twelve.
Gives the crew a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the price per acre, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price, so a shopped rate can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two 10,000 sq ft, 0.23-acre stops, one flat rate

Using this calculator's own shipped starting example:

A 10,000 sq ft, 0.23-acre lawn — open turf, no beds, no edging, and a short hop between stops — prices at $184.30 a month on a stop that takes 0.5 hours. Setting a flat rate per acre from that easy stop works out to $802.82 an acre a month.

Take the identical 10,000 sq ft, 0.23 acres of turf and put it on a harder lot instead — 350 sq ft of beds needing weeding, an edge-and-blow, and an 18-minute one-way drive — and the stop takes 2.4 hours, 4.8 times the easy stop's time on the identical turf acreage. Apply the $802.82-an-acre rate to this lot and it quotes $184.30 a month again, because the rate only knows acreage. This calculator prices the harder stop at $459.73 a month — the flat rate lands $275.43 a month short of that price, and $160.49 a month short of covering the stop's own break-even cost of $344.80. Same acreage, same flat rate, one lot that pays and one that loses money the moment the beds, the edging, and the drive show up.

Common questions

Why does a flat rate per acre get a lawn-care stop wrong?

Because the cost driver is the beds, the edging, and the drive, not the turf acreage. A 10,000 sq ft, 0.23-acre lawn that is open turf with no beds and a short hop between stops is a 0.5-hour mow. The identical 10,000 sq ft, 0.23-acre lot with 350 sq ft of beds needing weeding, an edge-and-blow, and an 18-minute one-way drive is a 2.4-hour stop -- 4.8 times the time, on the identical turf acreage. A flat per-acre rate charges both the same because it was set on acreage, not on beds, edging, or the drive.

What does a flat per-acre rate usually leave out entirely?

Bed weeding, edging and blowing, and the drive. A per-acre number has no line for square feet of beds at their own slower production rate, no line for the minutes an edge-and-blow takes, and no line for round-trip travel at all -- it prices the turf and assumes the rest of the stop away. On this calculator's own shipped starting example, that hidden work -- edging, beds, and the drive together -- is 79.1% of the total time on the job, on top of the mow itself.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped starting example: a 10,000 sq ft, 0.23-acre lawn that is open turf with no beds and a short hop between stops prices at $184.30 a month, on a stop that takes 0.5 hours. Setting a flat per-acre rate from that easy stop works out to $802.82 an acre a month. Apply that same rate to the identical 0.23 acres of turf on the harder lot -- 350 sq ft of beds, an edge-and-blow, and an 18-minute one-way drive, a 2.4-hour stop -- and it quotes $184.30 a month again, because the rate only knows acreage. This calculator prices that harder stop at $459.73 a month, so the flat rate lands $275.43 a month short of the calculator's own price, and $160.49 a month short of covering the stop's own break-even cost of $344.80. Same acreage, same flat rate, one lot that pays and one that loses money the moment the beds, the edging, and the drive show up.

Is a flat rate per acre ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of similar lots -- open turf, no beds to weed, no edge-and-blow, and a short hop from the stop before it -- a flat per-acre number can land close, because that is probably the lot the rate was set on. The risk is quoting a lot with beds, a full edge-and-blow, or a long drive the same way sight unseen, because the rate does not know the beds, the edging, or the drive until someone has walked the property, and by then the flat number has often already been quoted.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or fuel costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market or your fuel and equipment costs. It takes each service's quantity and production rate (turf, edging, beds, hedges, leaf cleanup), your visits per week, service weeks per year, round-trip travel, and your own wage, payroll burden, fuel, dump, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this stop -- the arithmetic a flat per-acre rate skips, not a market survey.

Open the Lawn Care Bid Calculator to price your own stop, or read the pricing walkthrough.

Verify every figure against your own payroll, fuel, insurance, and dump costs, and against a qualified professional, before relying on it or submitting a bid. This calculator vs. LMN by Granum

Two different shapes: LMN by Granum is an account-based platform for running a landscaping company's whole operation. This page is a free, private worksheet for one recurring stop — whether the price actually clears your production hours, travel, and margin, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

LMN by Granum is business management software built specifically for landscaping and lawn-care companies — not a generic construction or field-service tool. Long known as Landscape Management Network (LMN), it was brought together with SingleOps and Greenius under the shared Granum brand in 2025, while continuing under its own product name. It bundles estimating and budgeting, job costing, crew scheduling and time tracking, and payroll integration, used by a company's office staff and crews together across every property on the book, on an ongoing account. LMN's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page.

This calculator does none of that. It does not hold a customer list, schedule a crew across properties, or run payroll. It takes one recurring stop — each service split out with its own quantity and production rate (turf mowing, edging and blowing, bed weeding, hedge trim, leaf cleanup), visits per week, service weeks per year, round-trip travel time, loaded labor, fuel, dump, overhead, and the margin you intend to keep — and turns that into the price per visit, the in-season monthly, an honest annual at the growing-season week count rather than monthly × 12, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the stop loses money, plus a printable customer proposal with scope, deposit split, and a signature line. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

What you are trying to doWhere to do it
Price one recurring lawn-care stop correctly — turf, beds, edging, and windshield time each counted at their own rate. This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
Run estimates, job costing, and crew scheduling across an entire book of properties from one shared account. LMN, or a comparable landscape business platform — running the whole operation is not something this calculator does.
Understand why a price-per-acre rule misses beds and drive time. This calculator's own pricing walkthrough.
Have office staff, a sales rep, and crews working the same customer records and schedule together. LMN — built as an ongoing, account-based platform for exactly that job.
Run payroll or track time punches across a crew. LMN, or dedicated payroll software — this calculator has no time-clock or payroll feature.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool? This calculator: no. LMN is used through a paid, account-based subscription.

Most landscaping operations get different value from each: LMN (or a comparable platform) for running the company's whole estimating, scheduling, and job-costing operation as an ongoing account, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login check on whether one stop's price actually clears cost and margin before the bid goes out. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a customer record, a schedule, or a payroll entry.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or LMN by Granum?

They do different jobs. LMN by Granum — the software long known as Landscape Management Network, brought under the Granum brand alongside SingleOps and Greenius in 2025 — is business management software built specifically for landscaping and lawn-care companies: estimating and budgeting, job costing, crew scheduling and time tracking, and payroll integration, used by office staff and crews together across every property the company services, on an ongoing account. This calculator does none of that. It takes one recurring stop — each service's quantity and production rate (turf, edging, beds, hedges, leaf cleanup), visits per week, service weeks per year, round-trip travel, loaded labor, fuel, dump, overhead and target margin — and turns that into the price per visit, the in-season monthly, an honest annual at the growing-season week count, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away number below which the stop loses money, plus a printable customer proposal. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A landscaping company running estimates, crews, and job costing across its whole book of properties is better served by LMN or a comparable platform; an operator who wants an instant, private price for one stop before it is quoted is in the right place here.
